title: Resolving Event Noun Phrases to Their Verbal Mentions
research_question: Can event-denoting noun phrases be linked to their corresponding verbal event mentions across potentially long discourse distances using lexical, positional, syntactic, and pairwise-ranking information?
methodology: The authors formulate event-noun-phrase resolution as linking an event NP to a verbal mention and build a learning-based model with lexical, syntactic, and positional features. They encode syntactic relations with convolution tree kernels, combine these with flat features through a composite kernel, and apply a twin-candidate ranking SVM that compares antecedent candidates pairwise. Experiments use OntoNotes Release 2.0 English newswire and broadcast-news data, ten-fold cross-validation, precision/recall/F-score, ablation comparisons, learning curves, and paired significance testing.

key_findings.finding: Event noun phrases can refer to verbal mentions across substantially longer distances than the local windows commonly used for pronoun resolution, producing a much larger candidate set.
The flat-feature model obtained an F-score of 43.35, while combining the same features with the minimum-expansion tree kernel raised F-score to 59.01.
All reported composite-kernel configurations improved F-score by more than ten percentage points over the flat-feature baseline.

The minimum-expansion structural representation performed better than the more elaborate simple and full expansions, which the authors interpret as evidence that additional syntactic structure can introduce harmful noise.
Twin-candidate ranking improved the best composite model from 59.01 to 61.36 F-score, with precision of 66.41 and recall of 57.93.
The twin-candidate improvement was reported as statistically significant at the 5 percent level.

Learning-curve results suggested that performance was already relatively stable with a substantial subset of the available training data and that the largest training fractions were statistically indistinguishable.

limitations: The number of candidate verbs becomes very large because event-NP links may span long distances, increasing computational cost, especially for pairwise twin-candidate comparisons.
Evaluation is restricted to English OntoNotes 2.0 newswire and broadcast-news genres.
The task formulation focuses specifically on links between event noun phrases and verbal mentions rather than all possible cross-form event-coreference relations.
The model relies on automatic syntactic parsing and named-entity preprocessing, so upstream errors can affect resolution.
Explicit semantic-role and verb-frame information is not incorporated; the authors identify such semantic information as future work.
raw_claims: The paper studies resolution of event-denoting noun phrases to verbal mentions of the same event.
The OntoNotes-based data extraction produced 977 verbal-mention and event-NP links for the study.
The average sentence distance between linked mentions is reported as 2.97.
The candidate-generation setting yields roughly 30.49 verb candidates per training instance and 583.74 per test instance on average.
A most-recent-verb strategy is unsuitable because most noun phrases in the candidate space are not event anaphors and only a small fraction of verbs are referred to by event NPs.
The flat lexical, syntactic, and positional feature model reports an F-score of 43.35.
Adding a minimum-expansion tree kernel to the flat features raises F-score to 59.01.
More elaborate tree expansions perform worse than the minimum expansion in the reported experiments.
Pairwise twin-candidate ranking raises the best system's F-score to 61.36.
The authors propose richer semantic information, including semantic roles and verb frames, as a direction for improving the resolver.
